RAG: Retrieval Meets Generation
Every number on this page is read from the seminar's artifacts (bge-m3, bge-reranker-v2-m3 and a 3B ruadapt Qwen, run on the notebook's pipeline) or computed in the browser and checked against Python — nothing is typed in.

Author: Daria Andreeva

RAG Systems: The Beginning

A retriever, a generator, and five places between them that we can influence. Every stand on this page runs the seminar notebook's pipeline on one corpus: search, cosines and metrics are computed in the browser or read from the seminar's artifacts, and the answers are what the 3B model actually wrote.

RAG is not "connect a database to the model" but a pipeline of six blocks, where each one can be broken and each one can be improved separately.

We work with a dataset built from a Telegram channel, gonzo_ML, which I parsed in advance: posts about papers, mostly in Russian, often with English quotes inside. Some are a full review, some are one word.

Next to it, the "golden set": question–context pairs on which we count "hits". In my case the "context" is also the answer. The catch, which section 07 measures: the contexts are retold, not copied. So each question keeps the post it is about, and a hit is a document from that post.

The data for the whole seminar

Block 01 · the pipeline

RAG: simple and less simple

Simple: documents + question → LLM → answer. Less simple: the documents are first split and encoded into an index, the question is encoded by the same encoder, the search over the index returns the top-k, and only those get into the prompt. The five places we can influence are marked with numbers.

One query through the whole pipelinesearch · real; answer · the 3B model's

So far the pieces were assembled by hand. In practice they are combined into one RAG module with the LangChain Expression Language (LCEL): a declarative chain retriever -> prompt -> llm -> parser built with the | operator. Hover a line to see which step of the stepper it is.

Block 02 · what is indexed

  
Documents, chunks, vectors

  
To encode documents and queries we use BAAI/bge-m3 — a symmetric multilingual model that needs no special prefixes for queries. The documents go into Qdrant, in memory; the retriever is the store's as_retriever().

  

    
LangChain · the indexthe notebook's cells

    

      
qdrant.as_retriever() with no arguments — how many documents does it return for a query?

      

      

    

    
Four: LangChain's default k, for every retriever, BM25Retriever too. The first run of the notebook compared Qdrant at four against BM25 at ten. Everything on this page is a top-10.

  


  
Parent document

  
Now let's split everything into chunks: the parent-document retriever, which does well on long texts. Small children are what gets searched — a short piece is close to a short question; the parent it came from is what gets returned — the model needs the whole context.

  
  

    
Small children are searched, the parent is returnedbge-m3 · 120-character children

    

      
      

    

    

  

  

    
LangChain · ParentDocumentRetrieverthe notebook's cell

    

    
The children get their own collection. In the first run of the notebook they went into qdrant itself, next to the full documents — and the plain dense search above searched the 120-character pieces too.

  

  
Symmetric search. Index the questions to a text instead of the text itself: a user's question looks like a question, not like a paragraph of a review. The answer is linked to its question and comes along. Where the questions come from: an LLM per chunk, experts by hand, and above all the real queries of users, added as they come — the index grows with the product.

  






  
Block 03 · the search method

  
Sparse, dense, and both

  
Three families: sparse (TF-IDF, BM25 — they count word matches), dense (cosine between the encoder's vectors) and the ensemble (Reciprocal Rank Fusion — it adds up ranks, not scores). Each loses on its own kind of query; pick a question and see where.

  

    
Retrieval arenaBM25 in the browser · dense from the artifact

    

      

      
Pick a question — the gold post is green; or type your own text and press Enter. Free text works only for the lexical columns: the encoder cannot be run in the browser, its vectors for the fixed questions were computed in advance.

      

      
How each column is computed
        

          
tokens
lower case? No: text.split() — words are whatever stands between spaces, punctuation included. The lower-case column uses re.findall(r"\w+", text.lower()). 

          
BM25

            score(q,d)=
              ∑t∈qidf(t)·
              tf(t,d)·(k1+1)
              tf(t,d)+k1·(1−b+b·|d|/avgdl)
            
saturation in the term's frequency (k1=1.5) and a penalty for the document's length (b=0.75); the score has no upper bound

          
dense
score(q,d)=cos(e(q),e(d))
the vectors of the documents and of the fixed questions were computed in advance, so for free text this column is empty

          
ensemble
score(d)=
            ∑m∈retrieverswm60+rankm(d)
ranks are added, not scores: BM25, cosine and TF-IDF live on different scales

A question to the room

    
Why does the ensemble add up ranks and not the scores themselves?

      
The scores are not comparable: BM25 runs from 0 to infinity, cosine from −1 to 1. Normalising them on the fly is not honest (BM25 has no upper bound), while any method has a rank. The price: RRF does not know how far the first one is ahead of the second.

    
The notebook's cell. weights=[0.5, 0.5], and a constant c = 60 that is not in the call: it is the default.

  







  
Block 04 · before the search

  
Preprocessing the query

  
It often happens that users ask questions not at all the way we expect: with typos, incompletely, illiterately — and we need to be able to handle it (because we have no choice). Three tricks to make the query look more like what lies in the index, or to search not once but as many times as needed.


  
Query expansion

  
As a rule, we solve the problem of non-standard but complete queries by rephrasing the user's question. Left: the question searched as is; right: the 3B model's rephrasing, searched the same way.

  

    
The question and its rephrasing, searched the same waybge-m3 · rephrased by the 3B model

    

      
      

      

    

    

  


  
Rephrasing is often enough on its own: typos, slang and transliteration are fixed, and the question meets the words of the documents. It also has edge cases. The model rephrases what it understood, and a name it does not know, a word cut short or a word written as it sounds becomes something else — confidently and grammatically.

  

    
What rephrasing fixes and what it breaksBM25, lower case, in the browser

    

      
Tick the rows where the rephrasing changed what the user meant.

      

      

    

    

  


  
HyDE

  
Idea: instead of searching by the user's query directly, ask the LLM to generate a hypothetical answer — as if it were already in the knowledge base. The embedding of this hypothetical document is used as the search query.


Contrast with QE: QE fixes the form of the question (grammar, style), HyDE guesses the semantics of the answer. On short incomplete questions HyDE usually gives a bigger gain.

  
  

    
Search with the question, search with a hypothetical answerbge-m3 · hypothetical answer by the 3B model

    

      
Our questions are complete, and bge-m3 was trained on question–passage pairs. Will HyDE beat searching with the question itself?

      

      

        
        

        

        
the bet first

      

    

    

  

  
The price of HyDE in production: one more LLM call per query, before the search even starts — latency and tokens. And it amplifies the model's guess, right or wrong.


  
SelfQuery

  
SelfQuery. Part of the query is not about meaning but about the fields of the collection: a date, a genre, an author. Such things are not searched by cosine, they are filtered. In production an LLM extracts the fields by the collection's schema; here, rules, so that you can see exactly what should come out. Two collections: our posts, and a collection made for it.

FLARE

  
FLARE, forward-looking active retrieval: do not search once before generation, but write a sentence as a draft, look at the probabilities of its tokens, and if the confidence fell below a threshold, go search with this sentence as the query and rewrite it. The threshold is a budget: at zero there is no search at all and the made-up details stay; near one there is a search for every sentence.

  
  

    
Forward-looking active retrievalscripted

    

      
Scripted: the token probabilities and the retrieved documents are set in advance, on a synthetic shop FAQ.

      
Курьер опоздал, а один товар приехал разбитым. Что мне полагается и когда вернут деньги?

      

        

      
the model's answer (above each token, its probability)

        
log: generation → search → regeneration

      

    

    
Try θ = 0: no search at all, and the answer keeps plausible but made-up numbers — ordinary RAG without retrieval on demand. Try θ = 0.9: a search for every sentence, three retriever calls and three regenerations — expensive. The threshold is a budget.

  







  
Block 05 · after the search

  
Reranking

  
A reranker is a language model that takes two texts and returns how close they are. Cheap: select candidates with the bi-encoder and BM25; expensive: rerank only those with a cross-encoder, which sees the pair "query–document" as a whole. As the reranker we use a multilingual model trained for exactly this, BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3.

  
  

    
How many candidates to rerankbge-reranker-v2-m3 over the ensemble's pool

    

      
More candidates for the reranker: does quality keep growing all the way to 50?

Block 06 · generation

  
The prompt, and where hallucinations come from

  
The retriever has found something — from here on the prompt decides. The main source of hallucinations in RAG is a context that is not enough: the retriever brought the wrong thing or not all of it, and the model has to answer anyway. So the defence is built around the question "is the context enough?" — before generation, during, and after.


  

    
Prompt sandbox

    

      
The same question under three prompts: no context (closed book), the retrieved top-3, and the top-3 plus the line «Если в контексте нет ответа, явно скажи об этом». Every answer is the 3B model's, greedy; nothing is written by hand.

      
      
the prompt

        
the answer

      
The ten questions without an answer in the corpus, with the top-3 in the prompt. What does the line «Если в контексте нет ответа, явно скажи об этом» change?

      

    

    

  


  
A threshold on similarity

  
The most obvious filter: do not answer if the best cosine is below a threshold. Below — the best dense cosine for every question: the golden ones, and the ones the corpus cannot answer. Move the threshold and try to find a value that breaks neither group.

  

    
The best cosine per questionbge-m3 · top-1 over the documents

    

      
Is there a threshold that keeps all the golden questions and stops all the questions without an answer?

      

      

      

      

    

    

  


  
Thirty questions of one corpus happened to separate. In general they do not, and the reason is in which questions arrive. A synthetic example with the shapes that show up in practice: well-formed questions the collection answers score high, off-topic ones score low — and a threshold between them looks perfect. Then real traffic adds two more groups: answerable questions written badly (typos, two keywords instead of a sentence), whose best cosine drops, and unanswerable questions on the collection's topic, whose best cosine is as high as a real hit's, because their neighbours are about the same thing.

  

    
Why a threshold fails in generalsynthetic scores

    

      
Add both groups. Is there still a threshold that refuses fewer than 10% of the answerable questions and lets through fewer than 10% of the unanswerable ones?

CRAG: ask the model whether the context is enough

  
CRAG, corrective RAG: after getting the candidates, the LLM judges their relevance. If the context is irrelevant, the system switches to a fallback strategy — web search, another corpus, or refusing to answer. Here: the 3B model, one call, "yes" or "no" for the top-1 document.

  

    
"Is the context enough to answer?" — the 3B model on the top-1 document

    

      
How many of the ten questions without an answer does the check let through?

      

      
the bet first

    

    

  

  

    
Before generation
LLM judge "is the context enough for an answer?" (expensive, but works), metadata filters. A similarity threshold only as a rough first filter and only after checking it on your data; more often it is better not to use it.

    
During
Look at the logits: a low probability of the tokens is a signal of doubt (FLARE above). A logits processor forbids what must not be in the answer.

    
After
Prompt chaining: first pick quotes from the context, then answer only from them; an explicit "I don't know" in the instruction; a groundedness check with a second call.

  







  
Block 07 · how to measure

  
What counts as a hit

  
Three families of metrics, and each has its blind spot: distance metrics between texts need a reference and miss hallucinations; ranking metrics evaluate the retriever, not the system; LLM-based metrics evaluate everything but are unstable. And before any of them: what counts as a hit.

  
A hit is a proxy. "The retriever found the answer" is never observed directly; it is replaced by something that can be checked automatically, and the choice decides what the metric measures.


a hit is…needsbreaks when


metadata: the retrieved chunk has the id of the post (document, section, URL, product) labelled as the answerthe golden set written down as ids; the id carried by every chunkthe documents are re-split and a chunk loses its parent's id; the answer sits in two posts and one is labelled


text: the golden quote occurs in the retrieved text — exactly, or by fuzzy match above a thresholda quote per question, no idsthe quote was retold rather than copied; the threshold is set by taste


a model: an LLM reads the question and the chunk and says whether the chunk answersnothing labelled per documentthe judge is noisy and biased — the last part of this block


The first version of the notebook used the second proxy: a retrieved text is a hit if fuzz.partial_ratio(golden quote, text) >= 80. This page uses the first: the post id. On the same retrieved lists, the two can be compared pair by pair.

Ranking metrics

  
The retriever's output for one query. Drag the documents (or use the arrows), move k — the metrics are recomputed term by term. What all of them share: without a labelling of "what is relevant" none of them can be computed.

  

    
P@k, Hit@k, reciprocal rank, NDCG@k on a live outputcomputed in the browser

    

      

      

      

    

    
P@k does not distinguish the order inside the top-k; with one relevant post per question it stays near 1/k (above it only when the post was split into several documents), which is why the notebook reports Hit@k instead. MRR rewards the relevant document for being higher; NDCG@k does the same with a logarithmic discount and can work with graded relevance (0/1/2). All of them are silent about what the LLM will do with what was found.

LLM as a judge

  
A judge is a model with a prompt, and the prompt is a measuring instrument. Three ways to use it, and what a rubric needs:


schemewhat the judge doeswhen


pointwisescores one answer on a scale or by criteriaan absolute score is needed: monitoring in production


pairwisecompares two answers and picks the better oneA against B: steadier than a scale, but sensitive to the order


reference-basedcompares the answer with a reference onea set with references exists: regression tests


A rubric has four parts:


    

  1. criteria — independent axes; "quality" and "usefulness" are one axis counted twice;
    2. 

  2. a scale for each criterion: pass/fail, 1–5, a share;
    3. 

  3. anchors — what each mark means; a "5" without a description is not a criterion but a lottery;
    4. 

  4. edge cases — a partly correct answer, a contradictory context, a question outside the domain. Whatever is not written down, the judge decides by itself, and differently each time.
    5. 



The order of work: the rubric before the prompt → a pilot on contrasting examples → reasoning before the score → structured output → few criteria per call → freeze it before the mass run. Criteria drift as people label (Shankar et al., 2024): a rubric is versioned like a prompt.


biaswhat is knownhow to check it on your datahow to treat it


positionin pairwise the judge prefers the first answer; GPT-4 on MT-Bench is consistent under swapping in ≈ 65% of pairs, weaker judges less oftenevery pair in both orders; the share of disagreementsaverage over both orders; a disagreement is a tie


lengthan inflated answer with the same facts scores higher; GPT-4 is steadier than others, but not fullyinflate 10 answers without new facts, comparea brevity criterion in the rubric; length-controlled win rate


self-preferencea judge overrates answers of its own family: about 10 points of win rate for GPT-4blind labelling; a second judge of another familya judge of another family, or a specialised one (Prometheus 2)


noiseat T > 0, different scores for the same input; at T = 0, not zero eitherR repeats of one input, σjudgeT = 0 and measure the rest; average




The numbers are from Zheng et al. (2023) and Wang et al. (2023), for other people's judges on other tasks. Below — ours: two judges on twenty answers.
Calibrating on people: kappa. If 90% of the answers are good, a judge that always says "good" agrees with a person on 90% of them while telling nothing apart. Cohen's κ subtracts the agreement expected from random labels: κ=(po−pe)/(1−pe). Landis and Koch's reading: below 0.2 slight, 0.2–0.4 fair, 0.4–0.6 moderate, 0.6–0.8 substantial, above that almost perfect. On an ordinal scale (1–5) plain κ punishes "5 against 4" exactly as "5 against 1"; weighted κ with quadratic weights punishes by the square of the distance.

Block 08 · the roadmap

  
What in the end: where to start in each block

  
No block is there "just because": each has a default to start from and a lever to pull when the metrics on the golden set do not add up. The loop closes on validation by experts — and goes back to the index.

  

    

      
A quick checklist of basic RAG techniques and how to choose

      
    

  1. Are there external documents the correctness of the answer depends on?

      

    • Yes; is the volume of documents larger than the model's context window?

        

      • Yes → you need RAG, a retriever / chunking.
        • 

      • No → you can try to stuff all the documents into the system prompt.
        • 

      

      • 

    • No; we don't use contexts in generation
      • 

    

    2. 

  2. Is the query short and different from the wording of the documents?

      

    • Yes, slightly → think about different encoders, query expansion, a reranker.
      • 

    • Yes, strongly → most likely you should use symmetric search instead of asymmetric
      • 

    

    3. 

  3. Do you need citations / traceability?

      

    • Yes → do RAG (keeping the sources).
      • 

    

    4. 

  4. Domains with a high cost of error?

      

    • Yes → RAG + a strict instruction "rely only on the context".
      • 

    

    5. 


      
What to take away

      
    

  1. Five points of influence and the order in which they are turned: first the data and the index, then the search, then the prompt, and only then the model.
    2. 

  2. Every metric misses something — and the golden set, with what counts as a hit, is needed before the first experiment, not after.
    3. 

  3. A difference of one question on twenty is not a result.
    4.
